findings.headline: Sole cashable benefit identified is licensing savings, "a small saving", realised after implementation and a transitionary period
findings.detail: The sole cashable benefit identified is savings on existing software licensing from moving to a hosted solution on mainstream technology. However, the amount is not quantified (described only as 'a small saving'), and these savings will only be realised after implementation and a transitionary period. The council must fund the full cost of both systems during transition before any offsetting benefit arrives.
findings.matters: A council is committing significant capital and revenue with only one financial benefit and that benefit is unquantified, described as small, and delayed, creating a prolonged period where the investment has no offsetting return to the budget.
findings.figures: Licensing savings described as 'a small saving'; timing post-implementation and transitionary period; amounts not specified
findings.quote: will allow us to make a small saving on licensing we currently have in place to cover the incumbent system's infrastructure

findings.headline: Implementation delay beyond August 2028 would trigger renegotiation of incumbent supplier contract at higher cost
findings.detail: The council's existing support contract for the current system (Open Housing) has a fixed extension deadline of 31 March 2028. The council targets decommissioning by 31 August 2028, creating a 5-month window. If this target is missed, the council would need to renegotiate a further extension with the supplier at terms the supplier proposes.
findings.matters: Project schedule slippage creates unbudgeted cost risk: missing the decommissioning deadline would force the council to renegotiate supplier contract terms at potentially significantly higher cost.
findings.figures: Current contract extension deadline 31 March 2028; decommissioning target 31 August 2028; 5-month contingency window
findings.quote: Should we not be able to decommission the system by 31/08/2028, we face having to reach an agreement to extend the support. It is likely that any further extension would see a potential significant increase in cost and may also require us to upgrade the system again.

findings.headline: Cost-benefit analysis incomplete and full project costs not disclosed in business case
findings.detail: The council's cost-benefit analysis is still under development and will be refined through several iterations. The business case references draft costs in Appendix 3 but this appendix is not included in the published version (marked as Part 2 confidential information). Full costs will only emerge when suppliers submit tender responses.
findings.matters: A council is advancing a major capital procurement without having completed its own cost-benefit analysis or disclosing project costs, raising questions about financial planning and decision-making.
findings.figures: Draft costs in Appendix 3 (not disclosed); full costs to be determined at tender evaluation stage; revenue costs for first 7-year term to be included in supplier pricing
findings.quote: The cost benefit analysis is still currently being developed. Given the uncertainty of the outcome of the procurement process, this is a complex process and will develop over several iterations of this Business Case.

findings.headline: Council committing to multi-year capital and revenue expenditure with no immediate cashable benefits
findings.detail: The council is committing to significant capital costs for implementation plus ongoing annual revenue costs for a replacement housing management system over a 7-year initial contract term, extendable annually. The business case explicitly states there are no immediate cashable benefits, with only non-cashable benefits and software licensing savings to be realised only after implementation and a transitionary period.
findings.matters: A council is making a major multi-year financial commitment with material revenue budget implications but no offsetting financial returns in the short to medium term.
findings.figures: Initial contract period 7 years with annual extension options to maximum 21 years; support contract for existing system expires 31 March 2027 with 12-month extension option to 31 March 2028
findings.quote: There are no immediate cashable benefits arising from the business case. However, following implementation and a transitionary period, savings on existing software licensing will be realised

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Temporary borrowing from other councils reduced to £10m from £19m year-on-year
findings.detail: The council's reliance on short-term borrowing to manage cash flow decreased significantly during the year. This reduction of £9m represents a 47% decrease in temporary borrowing compared to the prior year end, suggesting improved cash flow management and reduced need for temporary funding solutions.
findings.matters: Reduction in short-term borrowing indicates improved liquidity and working capital management, reducing near-term refinancing risks.
findings.figures: Temporary borrowing £10m at 31 March 2026 vs £19m at 31 March 2025; reduction of £9m or 47.4%
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council had £10m in temporary loans from one local authority, compared to £19m at the previous year end 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council confirmed no breaches of prudential indicators for 2025-26 and reports adoption of prudent treasury approach
findings.detail: The council's treasury activity operated within all mandatory prudential limits during the year. Borrowing remained below the Capital Financing Requirement (£336.97m actual vs £400.87m CFR), fixed rate exposure was 97.04% against a 100% limit, and peak external borrowing reached £349.3m within the authorised limit of £430m.
findings.matters: Prudential compliance demonstrates the council's borrowing decisions remain affordable and sustainable within regulatory limits despite increased debt and capital activity.
findings.figures: External borrowing £336,971k vs CFR £400,871k; peak borrowing £349.3m vs authorised limit £430m; fixed rate exposure 97.04% vs upper limit 100%
findings.quote: None of the Prudential Indicators have been breached and a prudent approach has been taken in relation to investment activity with priority being given to security and liquidity over yield.

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Financing cost ratio for Non-HRA improved to 5.96% from estimated 7.52%; HRA ratio improved to 37.19% from estimated 44.46%
findings.detail: Despite increased borrowing during the year, the proportion of revenue budget required to meet borrowing costs came in significantly lower than estimated for both non-HRA and HRA. Non-HRA financing costs were £17.402m against estimated £20.535m, while HRA financing costs were £7.668m against estimated £7.407m. The council notes the overall revenue overspend was separately reported to Cabinet.
findings.matters: Better-than-expected debt service ratios suggest actual affordability is stronger than forecast, either due to conservative estimates or capital spending phasing improvements.
findings.figures: Non-HRA: 5.96% actual vs 7.52% estimated; HRA: 37.19% actual vs 44.46% estimated; Non-HRA financing costs £17.402m vs £20.535m estimate; HRA financing costs £7.668m vs £7.407m estimate
findings.quote: The overall revenue overspend compared to budget has been separately reported to Cabinet (30 June 2026) with reasons provided for the overspend.

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Non-HRA capital expenditure outturn of £55.75m exceeded January 2025 estimate of £48.16m by £7.58m
findings.detail: The council's capital spending on non-housing services ran significantly above its estimate. The council attributes this to additional schemes being approved and additional funding being awarded after the estimate was set in January 2025. The HRA capital programme came in under estimate at £13.67m against £16.04m estimate.
findings.matters: Capital overspends can signal accelerated spending, scope creep, or increased capital commitments that affect future debt service and spending plans.
findings.figures: Non-HRA: £55,747k actual vs £48,163k estimate (£7.584m or 15.8% overspend); HRA: £13,674k actual vs £16,040k estimate; Total: £69,421k actual vs £64,203k estimate
findings.quote: The outturn non-HRA capital spend for 2025/26 is higher than the original estimate due to additional schemes being approved and additional funding (grants etc) being awarded after January 2025.

findings.paper_title: TM REPORT - App 1 Annual TM Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's total external borrowing increased to £326.97m at 31 March 2026 with average debt rate rising from 4.49% to 4.86%
findings.detail: The council borrowed £65m in new funding during the year (£20m from PWLB and £45m from NWF) while repaying £43.454m in maturing loans. As a result of this net increase in borrowing, the average rate on the council's debt rose by 37 basis points, reflecting higher borrowing costs in the current interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Rising cost of debt service is a key affordability indicator for lenders assessing whether the council can service increased debt levels without revenue stress.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £305,425k (1 April 2025) → £326,971k (31 March 2026); average rate 4.49% → 4.86%; new borrowing £65,000k; maturing loans £43,454k
findings.quote: As a result of this borrowing, the average rate on the Council's debt increased slightly from 4.49% at 1 April 2025 to 4.86% at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Reduction in employers pension contributions of £1,604k achieved through triennial pension fund review, representing 87.8% of total achieved savings
findings.detail: The council achieved £1,604k from reduced employers pension contributions following the pension fund triennial review, marked as fully achieved. This single item accounts for £1,604k of the £1,820k total achieved savings.
findings.matters: A large one-off pension gain masks the underlying delivery rate of operational savings plans; the council's 57.4% achievement rate is heavily dependent on non-recurring pension fund benefit
findings.figures: £1,604k achieved; represents 87.8% of total £1,820k achieved savings
findings.quote: Reduction in employers pension contributions as a result of triennial review of pension fund Other 1,604 Achieved 1,604 0

findings.headline: Homelessness service reform not achieved; £100k shortfall on planned prevention and accommodation redesign
findings.detail: The transformation initiative to reform homelessness services by focusing on prevention and moving from temporary accommodation (hotels and B&Bs) to leased private sector accommodation is marked 'Not Achieved' with £100k shortfall.
findings.matters: Undelivered homelessness reform leaves the council committed to continuing high-cost temporary accommodation spending, indicating underlying demand pressure not being addressed
findings.figures: £100k shortfall
findings.quote: Reforming the model for delivering homelessness services. Focus on prevention and moving away from temporary emergency accommodation through use of hotels and B&Bs.

findings.headline: In-house residential care homes for children not achieved; full £548k shortfall after planned September 2026 opening
findings.detail: The scheme to develop small care homes for children in-house, intended to open in September 2026, is marked 'Not Achieved' with zero current-year savings and the full £548k shortfall. This was a transformation initiative aimed at reducing reliance on independent agencies.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver major transformation schemes suggests execution or capacity constraints that affect the council's ability to reshape service delivery and reduce long-term cost exposure
findings.figures: £548k shortfall on £548k proposal
findings.quote: In house residential provision through the development of small care homes for children. Plan to open first in Sept 2026.

findings.headline: Savings proposals tracking £738k shortfall against £3.17m 2026/27 target, with 20.4% of proposals not achieved
findings.detail: The council planned £3,170k in savings proposals. As of October Cabinet, achievement stands at 57.4% with £1,820k achieved, 22.1% (£701k) in progress, and 20.4% (£648k) not achieved, leaving £738k undelivered against the target.
findings.matters: An undelivered savings plan creates a funding gap that the council must fill from reserves, additional cuts, or carry forward, signalling whether its financial planning is realistic
findings.figures: £3,170k original target; £738k shortfall; 57.4% achievement; 20.4% not achieved (£648k)
findings.quote: Not Achieved 648 20.4%

findings.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary
findings.headline: Corporate budget underspending by £719k (1.4% saving against £50,483k budget)
findings.detail: Non-service corporate costs are projected to underspend by £719k. While this demonstrates some budget control in back-office functions, the saving is insufficient to offset the schools overspend, leaving the council with a net budget pressure of £5,185k.
findings.matters: Corporate underspends provide offset to service pressures and demonstrate budgetary discipline, but the scale of the schools overspend means the net position remains a material overspend that will need to be managed through reserves or further action.
findings.figures: Budget £50,483k, Projected outturn £49,764k, Underspend £719k (-1.4%)

findings.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary
findings.headline: Overall council budget projected to overspend by £5,185k (1.7% of £308,908k budget)
findings.detail: The total council budget is forecast to outturn at £314,093k against a budget of £308,908k for 2026/27. The 1.7% overspend of £5,185k represents a material shortfall across all services and corporate costs combined.
findings.matters: The overall budget position determines whether the council can deliver its service plan and maintain financial sustainability. A material overspend indicates the budget is not being delivered as planned and will require reserve action or further savings.
findings.figures: Budget £308,908k, Projected outturn £314,093k, Variance £5,185k (1.7%)

findings.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary
findings.headline: Schools budget projected to overspend by £5,352k (5.4% of £98,524k budget)
findings.detail: Schools and non-delegated school budgets are forecast to outturn at £103,876k against a budget of £98,524k. This £5,352k overspend is the largest single service variance and accounts for the majority of the overall council budget pressure.
findings.matters: Schools overspends are a leading indicator of financial stress and typically trigger reserve drawdowns or mid-year service reductions. At 5.4%, this variance significantly exceeds inflation and indicates material service cost pressures.
findings.figures: Budget £98,524k, Projected outturn £103,876k, Variance £5,352k (5.4%)

findings.paper_title: REPLACEMENT OF COUNCIL HOUSING MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
findings.headline: Housing management system replacement to be funded from Housing Revenue Account and reserves, with final costs reported January 2027
findings.detail: The council plans to fund capital and revenue costs for a replacement housing management system from the Housing Revenue Account's future budgets and reserves. Specific costs are contained in confidential appendices. Final costings and the project's organizational impact will be presented to Cabinet in January 2027.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders track capital investment plans and reserve utilization to assess the sustainability of councils' finances
findings.figures: None disclosed (confidential appendix)
findings.quote: The bulk of the costs will be funded by the Housing Revenue Account and costs are being built into its revenue and capital budgets for future years along side use of reserves.

findings.headline: Council's outstanding borrowing stood at £336.9m at average rate of 4.86% at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: At year-end, the council held £336.9m in borrowing at an average cost of 4.86%, against £21.0m in investments earning an average return of 3.68%.
findings.matters: Finance directors monitor the absolute debt position and cost structure; lenders need to understand the council's borrowing exposure and debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: £336.9m borrowing at 4.86% average; £21.0m investments at 3.68% average
findings.quote: The Council's outstanding borrowing at 31 March 2026 was £336.9m at an average rate of 4.86% and the Council held £21.0m in investments at an average rate of 3.68%.

findings.headline: Council confirmed compliance with treasury limits and Prudential Indicators throughout 2025/26
findings.detail: The annual report confirms that the council complied with treasury limits and Prudential Indicators during the financial year, meaning it remained within its legal borrowing parameters and prudence thresholds.
findings.matters: Breach of prudential limits signals severe financial stress; confirmation of compliance is the baseline assurance both the council and its lenders require.
findings.figures: None reported
findings.quote: The report also reports on the risk implications of treasury decisions and transactions and confirms compliance with treasury limits and Prudential Indicators.

findings.headline: Internal audit review of treasury management returned no significant issues
findings.detail: The council's treasury management strategy and procedures are audited annually. The latest review was positive with no significant issues raised, confirming the control environment for borrowing and investment is sound.
findings.matters: Finance directors monitor audit outcomes as a key indicator of control quality and operational competence in treasury management; audit findings affect confidence in reported figures.
findings.figures: None reported
findings.quote: The Council's treasury management strategy and procedures are audited annually and the latest internal audit review was positive with no significant issues raised.

findings.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary
findings.headline: Corporate income projections slashed by £28.2m from budgeted £29.3m to £1.1m
findings.detail: Corporate income is now forecast at only £1,077k compared to budgeted £29,271k, a shortfall of £28,194k. This is offset by equivalent expenditure cuts, keeping net position neutral, but the scale of income reduction is extraordinary.
findings.matters: A £28m drop in corporate income expectations signals either loss of expected revenue sources or major budget reclassification; either way, it indicates the council's income base is less stable than budgeted
findings.figures: £28,194k reduction in income (from £29,271k to £1,077k)

findings.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspending by £442k on the council's largest service budget
findings.detail: Adult Social Care and Homelessness, budgeted at £67,754k (the largest service budget), is forecast to overspend by £442k (0.7%). This is the largest absolute overspend in the services section.
findings.matters: ASC is nationally a growing cost area; overspends here are significant given budget size and reflect sector-wide demand pressures that raise questions about future financial sustainability
findings.figures: £442k overspend (0.7%) on £67,754k budget

findings.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary
findings.headline: Planning service shows 2.2% overspend, the highest percentage variance across services
findings.detail: Planning, Public Protection and Countryside services are forecast to overspend by £268k against a budget of £12,213k. This is the largest percentage variance in the services section and points to specific cost pressures.
findings.matters: Concentrated overspends in individual services may indicate management control issues or unexpected cost drivers that could spread to other areas
findings.figures: £268k overspend (2.2%) on £12,213k budget

findings.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary
findings.headline: Council budget overspend of £510k worsens from previous forecast of £108k
findings.detail: Projected Council Budget outturn is £309,415k against budget of £308,905k, a £510k overspend (0.2%). This represents a deterioration of £402k from the previous position. The position is getting worse, not better.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand trajectory—a deteriorating position suggests budget control is slipping and may require drawing on reserves or immediate corrective action
findings.figures: £510k overspend against £309m budget (0.2%), versus £108k previous

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Waste and Recycling Budget and Costs - July 2026
findings.headline: First full year (2025/26) balanced budget rests on £2m Extended Producer Responsibility grant described as uncertain
findings.detail: Service reported balanced budget at 2025/26 year-end: actual costs £8.678m against budget £8.7m. This required £2m pEPR grant funding (out of £2.4m received; £0.4m set aside in reserve). Without grant, costs would have been £10.7m. Council acknowledges future pEPR funding levels are uncertain and whether it will impact Welsh Government's future funding to councils.
findings.matters: Reported balanced budget masks underlying costs of £10.7m that would be unaffordable without continued uncertain grant funding
findings.figures: Reported cost £8.678m; pEPR grant £2m used (£2.4m total received); underlying cost without pEPR £10.7m; budget £8.7m
findings.quote: What is uncertain is how much that funding will be, and whether it impacts in anyway on WG's future funding to Council's in Wales.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Waste and Recycling Budget and Costs - July 2026
findings.headline: Service overspent by £2m–£3m in transition year (2024/25) on budget the council knew was underfunded
findings.detail: Service overspent by £800k in 2023/24 against £7.2m budget. Council chose not to address this shortfall when setting 2024/25 budget at £7.2m. In transition year, actual costs were £10.4m (£9.2m net of £1.2m one-off income), producing reported overspend of £2m (£3.2m excluding one-off income). Overspend driven by agency staff, overtime, and temporary vehicle hire during operational transition.
findings.matters: A £2–3m overspend following a consciously underfunded budget indicates control issues and service delivery risk
findings.figures: 2024/25 budget £7.2m; actual costs £10.4m; reported overspend £2m (£3.2m before one-off income); prior underfunding £800k
findings.quote: Note that we knew that the waste service was under-funded by £800k but we chose not to address that in the budget for 2024/25 for the reasons explained above.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Waste and Recycling Budget and Costs - July 2026
findings.headline: Capital project overran approved budget by £1.5m, funded partly by £6.4m prudential borrowing
findings.detail: Initial estimate from 2018 was £12.4m. Final business case budget was £21.6m, with additional £1.3m approved October 2024 for total approved budget of £22.9m. Actual outturn was £24.4m. Funded through £6.4m of service-funded prudential borrowing, £13m Welsh Government grants, £3m general capital funding, and £1.9m reserves.
findings.matters: A £1.5m capital overrun (6.5%) signals project delivery risk, and the council must service £6.4m of borrowed capital
findings.figures: Approved budget £22.9m; Actual £24.4m; Prudential Borrowing £6.4m; WG Grants £13m
findings.quote: The project had been in the planning since 2018 with an initial capital cost of £12.4m. As is often the case with significant and complex capital projects that span over several years, the project had evolved over time and the capital costs changed as a result.

findings.paper_title: App 2 - Denbighshire CC Final Audit of Accounts Report 2022-23
findings.headline: Related party disclosure incomplete; elected member failed to declare directorships in organisations with council contracts
findings.detail: Testing identified one elected member who had failed to declare directorships in two organisations; review found transactions between the council and both organisations that should have been disclosed in the related party notes. Another member's declaration was not available at time of audit. This indicates weak governance controls over member declarations and potential transparency failures.
findings.matters: Incomplete related party disclosures represent a governance and transparency failure that concerns lenders. They obscure potential conflicts of interest and may indicate weaker oversight of member conduct and council spending.
findings.figures: One elected member's undeclared directorships in two organisations; transactions identified but not originally disclosed
findings.quote: One elected member had failed to declare their directorship in two organisations. Review identified transactions between the Council and both organisations, which should have been included in the disclosures in Note 32.

findings.paper_title: App 2 - Denbighshire CC Final Audit of Accounts Report 2022-23
findings.headline: Audit encountered significant difficulties reconciling transaction populations; financial ledger structure required manual combination of multiple reports
findings.detail: The audit team encountered significant difficulties reconciling populations for employee benefit expenses, fees and charges income, and other service expenditure. The financial ledger structure did not allow a single auditable population to be formed, requiring many reports to be generated and manually combined, consuming considerable time from both audit and finance staff.
findings.matters: This indicates fundamental weaknesses in the council's financial ledger and reporting controls, making it difficult to verify the accuracy and completeness of financial statements. It suggests the finance function lacks robust systems for transaction classification and reporting.
findings.figures: Not quantified, but described as requiring 'considerable amount of time' from both audit and finance teams
findings.quote: During the audit, the audit team encountered significant difficulties in reconciling populations for several classes of transaction including employee benefit expenses, fees, charges and other service income and other service expenditure. The structure of the financial ledger did not allow for a single population to be formed for the transaction lines within Note 5 to the financial statements. Many reports had to be generated from the ledger and combined, to create one transaction level population that was auditable.

findings.paper_title: App 2 - Denbighshire CC Final Audit of Accounts Report 2022-23
findings.headline: Material asset disposal not accounted for until two years after the event
findings.detail: An asset disposed of in the 2020-21 financial year was not accounted for by the council until 2022-23, requiring a £12.865 million correction across multiple years. This multi-year latency indicates weak asset disposal controls and reconciliation processes.
findings.matters: The delayed recognition of a major asset disposal suggests poor controls over fixed asset accounting and the completeness of financial records, both critical to lenders assessing financial management quality.
findings.figures: £12,865,000 adjustment for prior-year asset disposal; affected both 2021-22 and 2022-23 accounts
findings.quote: Asset disposed of in the 2020-21 financial year, but the disposal was not accounted for until the 2022-23 financial year.

findings.paper_title: App 2 - Denbighshire CC Final Audit of Accounts Report 2022-23
findings.headline: Audit completion massively delayed: 20 months overdue from original November 2023 deadline
findings.detail: The audit report, dated July 2026, was originally due in November 2023. The delay has been driven by significant accounting problems requiring extensive investigation, including complex capital accounting issues, difficulties reconciling transaction populations, and issues with valuations and asset disposals that took considerable audit team time to resolve.
findings.matters: A 20-month audit delay signals either severe accounting control problems or an unmanageable finance function, both of which concern lenders. It prevents timely financial reporting and delays stakeholder access to verified accounts. The council's inability to maintain clean, reconcilable records suggests systemic control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Original deadline: November 2023; Actual issue date: July 2026
findings.quote: We are aiming to certify your accounts in July 2026. This is significantly later that the original deadline of November 2023.

findings.paper_title: App 2 - Denbighshire CC Final Audit of Accounts Report 2022-23
findings.headline: Qualified audit opinion issued due to unquantified errors in asset valuations and revaluation reserves
findings.detail: The auditor has issued a qualified (rather than clean) opinion on the accounts because the council has incompletely and incorrectly recorded historical cost asset information and revaluation movements that cannot be quantified. The errors may date back to 2007-08 and affect both the revaluation reserve (£226.6m) and capital adjustment account (£233.3m). The council has been unable to determine the full value of the misstatement despite attempting a full review of asset movements since 2007-08.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion is a material red flag to lenders about the reliability of the council's financial statements and the effectiveness of its controls. The fact that systematic errors dating back 16 years remain unresolved indicates fundamental weaknesses in asset accounting governance.
findings.figures: Revaluation reserve £226,614,000; Capital adjustment account £233,316,000; uncorrected difference between fixed asset register and financial ledger of £8.9 million as at 31 March 2023
findings.quote: Due to incomplete historical information, it has not been possible to determine when these issues first arose. However, they may date back to 2007-08, when the Revaluation Reserve was introduced by the Code of Practice on Local Authority Accounting in the United Kingdom. The Council is currently analysing its accounting records to correct for this matter but to date has been unable to quantify the full value of the misstatement.

findings.headline: Statutory service cost pressures growing faster than available funding
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly flags concerns about increased pressures and growing demand in Social Care and Education, with funding failing to keep pace with inflationary, service and demographic pressures. Additional Learning Needs (ALN) demands are increasing in both volume and complexity. The council is setting aside additional reserves to address these pressures, signalling they expect continued strain.
findings.matters: Statutory services (social care and education) must be funded. If costs are growing faster than funding and cannot be constrained, the council faces structural budget pressure that will require further savings or reserve depletion in coming years.
findings.figures: £1.27m set aside to support ALN pressures for 2026/27
findings.quote: This remains a challenging financial period and some specific service issues, along with inflationary pressures across all services, are becoming increasingly hard to finance as our funding fails to keep up with inflationary, service, and demographic pressures.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection shortfall of £939k from rising historic debt
findings.detail: The Council Tax collection shortfall is mainly due to increasing historic Council Tax debt (more than 12 months overdue) requiring higher bad debt provisions. This collection trend is seen across Wales. While in-year collection remains strong at 96.88% (3rd highest in Wales), the historic debt problem represents a structural cash flow and collection issue.
findings.matters: Historic debt buildup indicates weakening collection performance and cash flow pressure. The pattern is not council-specific but systemic across Wales, suggesting potential structural issues in council finances across the region.
findings.figures: £939k shortfall, in-year collection 96.88% (3rd highest in Wales)
findings.quote: there is a shortfall in Council Tax collection of £939k. This is mainly due to an increase in historic Council Tax debt (due more than 12 months ago) and the resulting need to increase our provision for bad debt. This trend has been seen across Wales.

findings.headline: Schools moved to £2.457m deficit despite £5.2m additional council investment
findings.detail: Schools collectively drew down £3.061m from reserves during the year, moving from £604k surplus to £2.457m deficit. The number of schools in deficit rose to 25 from 22 in the previous year. The CFO notes schools are likely to face significant financial challenges in 2026/27 and beyond, reflecting wider national pressures in Wales.
findings.matters: Despite substantial council investment, schools are still drawing down reserves and increasing deficit balances. This indicates fundamental structural pressure in education funding that the council cannot contain, and represents growing financial risk.
findings.figures: £2.457m deficit carried forward (from £604k surplus), £3.061m reserve drawdown, £5.2m additional investment, 25 schools in deficit (up from 22)
findings.quote: The overall schools' balances carried forward into 2026/27 is a deficit of £2.457m, compared with balances brought forward into 2025/26 of £604k, which means schools have collectively drawn down £3.061m resulting in an overall deficit position.

findings.headline: School Balances recovered from £604k deficit to £2.5m positive in one year
findings.detail: School reserves swung from a £604k cumulative deficit at 31 March 2025 to a £2,457k positive balance at 31 March 2026, driven by a £3,061k in-year transfer. This sharp reversal suggests either clawback of previous deficits or a deliberate injection to stabilize school finances.
findings.matters: School deficits are a leading indicator of broader pressure on education budgets; the reversal is positive but the speed and magnitude raises questions about sustainability and whether primary budget pressure merely shifted to the council's account
findings.figures: Moved from (£604k) deficit to £2,457k positive, driven by £3,061k transfer

findings.headline: Coastal Defence capital reserve reached £16.3m and absorbed £2.7m in the year
findings.detail: The Coastal Defence scheme reserve is now the council's largest single capital earmark at £16,308k, having grown from £13,606k with a £2,702k in-year transfer. This multi-year build suggests an ongoing, material capital commitment to coastal protection infrastructure.
findings.matters: A lender assessing long-term financial capacity needs to know the funding certainty and end-date of a commitment this large; if grant-dependent, a withdrawal or reduction poses refinancing risk
findings.figures: £16,308k at 31 March 2026, £2,702k added in-year
findings.quote: Capital Schemes: Coastal Defence (10,539) (3,067) (13,606) (2,702) (16,308)

findings.headline: ALN Reforms reserve reached £2.1m after absorbing £1.3m transfer in a single year
findings.detail: The Additional Learning Needs Reforms reserve grew from £825k to £2,095k in 2025-26, with a transfer of £1,270k. This substantial in-year concentration suggests the council is funding anticipated statutory costs for implementing new special education provision rules.
findings.matters: Large earmarks for statutory demand (especially education) that build faster than planned indicate either unknown cost magnitude or compressed implementation timelines; a lender needs to know if the reserve will prove sufficient
findings.figures: £2,095k total reserve, £1,270k added in-year alone

findings.headline: Denbighshire created a £1.5m Council Tax reserve in 2025-26, with no prior year provision
findings.detail: A new Council Tax reserve of £1,500k appeared in 2025-26 with no previous balance. This large, single-year creation is unusual and suggests the council anticipated or encountered either council tax collection volatility, revaluation impacts, or exemptions/appeals that required a dedicated buffer.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand why council tax income was treated as variable enough to warrant a £1.5m reserve; this could flag either collection problems or structural income uncertainty
findings.figures: £1,500k transfer into new Council Tax reserve in 2025-26

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Coastal defence capital scheme involves approved borrowing with future repayment obligations
findings.detail: The Capital Financing budget includes estimated borrowing costs for a coastal defence scheme. The council has committed to repayment in line with an approved schedule and is setting aside reserves to meet those repayments as they fall due.
findings.matters: Capital borrowing creates future revenue obligations; lenders track councils' aggregate capital commitments and whether reserve levels can sustain repayment schedules.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: the budget includes estimated borrowing costs for the coastal defence scheme; in line with the approved repayment schedule, funds are set aside in reserve to meet future repayments

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Education Service faces £1.27m of ongoing Additional Learning Needs pressures
findings.detail: Education Service pressures in ALN have been partially offset by £785k GwE cost repayment, but the council has set aside £1.27m to reserves explicitly to support ALN pressures going forward. This signals demand-led cost growth requiring ongoing budget support.
findings.matters: Growing ALN demand pressures are a structural cost that will recur; relying on reserves to fund them signals structural underfunding of this area.
findings.quote: Pressures in Additional Learning Needs offset by receipt of repayment of costs from GwE (£785k) and effective use of grants. £1.270m set-aside to reserves to help pressures in Additional Learning Needs

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Headline underspend masks reliance on £3.771m one-off Welsh Government grant
findings.detail: The reported £998k underspend in Corporate & Miscellaneous largely reflects one-time receipt of £3.771m Welsh Government grant for employee costs. The paper does not indicate this funding will recur, meaning the underlying budget position is materially weaker than the outturn headline suggests.
findings.matters: One-off grants mask structural budget gaps; their absence next year would expose whether the council's baseline operations can sustain themselves.
findings.quote: Budget underspend is due to receipt of a Welsh Government grants (£3.771m) to support the Council with additional employee costs

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Highways service has not delivered £327k of planned savings: £212k in Public Conveniences, £115k in structure costs
findings.detail: Highways reports continuing difficulty achieving £212k of planned savings in Public Conveniences and £115k in structure costs. These delays indicate struggle to implement efficiency measures that were budgeted as part of the council's savings plans.
findings.matters: Consistent failure to deliver budgeted savings signals operational difficulty executing planned efficiency and raises risk on future savings assumptions.
findings.quote: Budget pressure due to continuing process to achieve saving proposals in the Public Conveniences service (£212k), to achieve savings in structure costs (£115k)

findings.paper_title: FINAL OUTTURN - App 2 Service Variance Narrative 25-26
findings.headline: Planning service reporting £623k shortfall in car parking income
findings.detail: The Planning, Public Protection and Countryside service underperformed on car parking revenue expectations by £623k. This was the primary driver of the service's £424k overspend position, only partially offset by underspends in transport and grant income elsewhere in the service.
findings.matters: A material shortfall on a controllable, sustainable revenue stream suggests demand weakness or collection/pricing issues that will persist unless addressed.
findings.quote: Budget pressure from shortfalls in car parking income (£623k) partly offset by underspends in school transport

findings.headline: Council's unearmarked reserves stand at only 2.14% of the net revenue budget, limiting shock absorption
findings.detail: The Council Fund balance is £6.6m, which represents 2.14% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget of £309m. The council acknowledges that "Due to inflation in recent years being at high levels the Council's net revenue budget has increased and the value of the unearmarked reserve, relative to net budget has been eroded" and states it is an aim "to continue to increase the level of un-earmarked reserves over the medium term where possible."
findings.matters: At only 2.14% of budget, the council has minimal buffer for unexpected cost pressures or revenue shortfalls. Any significant adverse event (grant cut, cost overrun) would force either immediate service cuts or drawing on earmarked reserves.
findings.figures: Council Fund balance £6.6m; net revenue budget 2026/27 £309m; unearmarked reserves as % of budget 2.14%
findings.quote: £6.6m is 2.14% of the net revenue budget for 2026/27 at £309m and it is an aim to continue to increase the level of un-earmarked reserves over the medium term where possible.

findings.headline: Children's placements and homelessness costs are rising faster than inflation and are difficult to control
findings.detail: The council identifies Children's Services placements as having demand that is "difficult to forecast" with "complexity of needs coupled with inflation" driving up costs significantly. Welsh Government's priority to eliminate private profit from looked-after children's care is driving costs up in advance of legislative deadlines. For homelessness, a "significant increase in the number of people presenting as homeless in recent years" has led to "significant additional cost, particularly in relation to temporary accommodation." While workstreams aim to reduce costs, "the situation can change quickly."
findings.matters: These are statutory services where demand and cost pressures are largely outside the council's control. Unbudgeted cost escalation in these areas would directly impact the council's ability to balance budgets and would require draw-down of reserves or cuts to other services.
findings.figures: No specific quantum given; identified as an emerging risk with the caveat that homelessness temporary accommodation costs are "significant" and that workstreams show "positive results to reduce the costs"
findings.quote: Children's Services Placements – demand is difficult to forecast, complexity of needs coupled with inflation have driven up costs significantly in recent years. WG have set a priority of eliminating private profit from the care of looked after children, this is having an impact on the market in Wales by driving up costs in advance of those legislative deadlines.

findings.headline: An £11m funding gap remains for 2027/28 even with a 5.9% Council Tax rise; 19% increase would be needed to avoid service cuts
findings.detail: For 2027/28, a mid-range Council Tax increase of 5.9% would yield only £5m and address roughly a third of the funding gap, leaving an £11m shortfall. The council would need to raise Council Tax by 19% to balance the budget without service reductions. No indication of Welsh Government funding levels beyond 2026/27 has been provided.
findings.matters: The council faces difficult and politically constrained choices to close a material gap. A lender needs to understand whether the council has credible plans to close the gap and whether reliance on service cuts or reserves will erode financial resilience.
findings.figures: 2027/28 funding gap £11m; Council Tax increase assumption 5.9% yielding £5m; Council Tax increase required to balance without cuts 19%
findings.quote: A mid-range assumption of a Council Tax increase of 5.9% for 2027/28 yields an additional £5m and addresses roughly a third of the funding gap, the remaining gap is £11m. Council Tax would need to be set at 19% in theory to set a balanced budget with no reductions to budgets.

findings.headline: Cumulative budget pressures of £94m over four years are unprecedented for this council
findings.detail: The council faced £94m in cumulative pressures from 2023/24 to 2026/27, with Welsh Government funding covering only just over half (£51m) and the council forced to find £25m in savings or service reductions. The council explicitly states: 'The Council has not experienced sustained pressures at such a high level before.'
findings.matters: Unprecedented scale of pressures indicates structural stress in the council's financial position and suggests the underlying drivers (demand, pay inflation, service complexity) are not being resolved, only managed year-to-year.
findings.figures: Cumulative pressures £94m; Welsh Government funding £51m; savings/measures £25m; Council Tax increases £18m
findings.quote: The cumulative pressures over the 4-year period from 2023/24 to 2026/27 total £94m. The Council has not experienced sustained pressures at such a high level before.

findings.headline: School reserves have fallen from £5.7m to a projected deficit of £5.2m, with 22 schools in financial deficit
findings.detail: Combined school reserves have deteriorated from £5.7m in 2020/21 to £0.6m in 2024/25, with a forecast deficit of £5.190m by April 2026. The number of schools in financial deficit has risen from 2 in 2021/22 to 22 in 2024/25. The council acknowledges it is "increasingly concerned about the pressure on school finances" and the rate reserves are reducing.
findings.matters: Schools operating with negative reserves cannot sustain operations and signal structural dysfunction in education funding. This constrains the council's ability to support education and its financial stability more broadly.
findings.figures: School reserves: £5.7m (2020/21) → £0.6m (2024/25) → -£5.190m (April 2026 forecast); schools in deficit: 2 (2021/22) → 22 (2024/25)
findings.quote: Combined level of School Reserves (at year end in £m): 5.7, 12.4, 8.9, 3.6, 0.6; Combined use of reserves during the year (in £m): Increase 6.7, 3.5, 5.3, 3; Number of schools in financial deficit: 8, 2, 3, 13, 22

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: Chief Executive and Senior Leadership Team were both changed during 2023–2024, introducing execution risk during financial stress
findings.detail: The council underwent significant leadership turnover: the Chief Executive changed recently, the Senior Leadership Team was restructured in 2023 with several senior officers new to post, and the Cabinet was also relatively new when formed in 2022. The council acknowledges this created risk to the council's budget-setting ability during a period when financial stability was already strained.
findings.matters: Leadership churn during financial distress increases the risk of execution failure. A lender needs confidence that leadership has both the experience and institutional knowledge to navigate sustained budget pressures.
findings.figures: CEO change recent; SLT restructure 2023; Cabinet formed 2022
findings.quote: There has been a change in the Council's Chief Executive Officer in recent months which could potentially have increased the Council's risk. The restructure of the Senior Leadership Team in 2023 meant that some Senior Officers were new into post.

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: Financial Regulations have not been updated since the finance system change in April 2024
findings.detail: The council implemented a new financial system in April 2024 that replaced all legacy financial IT systems. A review and update of Financial Regulations was planned for late 2025/26 but has not been completed. The Finance Team lacks capacity to do it.
findings.matters: Procedures that do not match the systems they are supposed to govern create control gaps and audit risk. A 16-month delay in completing this after system implementation is a material governance weakness.
findings.figures: Finance system change: April 2024; review still pending as of May 2026 (13 months after implementation)
findings.quote: A new finance system was implemented during April 2024 which replaced all our financial IT systems. Admittedly it has not been possible to complete the regular review and update of Financial Regulations. There has not been the capacity within the Finance Team to complete the review.

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: Reserves only recently recovered from a prolonged depletion, and growth depends on one-off Welsh Government funding
findings.detail: Denbighshire's reserve position was negative for years as the council drew them down to cover in-year overspends. Recent growth in 2024/25 and 2025/26 came entirely from additional one-off Welsh Government funding, not from operational improvement or structural balance.
findings.matters: If reserves are recovering only because of one-off funding rather than structural budget balance, they remain vulnerable to the next pressure. A lender needs to know whether the council can actually build sustainable financial strength.
findings.figures: Reserve growth in 2024/25 and 2025/26 from Welsh Government funding only
findings.quote: Reserves have grown modestly during 2024/25 and 2025/26, due to additional in year funding from Welsh Government. Though the trend before that was negative as the Council has had to use reserves to cover in year unplanned overspends.

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: The 2026/27 budget relies on £3m of undelivered savings, with reserves as the backstop if they fail
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget assumes delivery of £3m in savings that have not yet been identified or secured. The council's explicit strategy is to draw on reserves to cover any shortfall if these savings cannot be delivered in-year.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings targets combined with two years of recent overspending mean reserves are the only buffer between budget balance and a formal notice of distress. If reserves are consumed, capacity to absorb any further pressure vanishes.
findings.figures: £3m savings target for 2026/27
findings.quote: 2026/27 budget contains £3m of savings to be realised. Reserves provide a level of mitigation should savings not be deliverable in year

findings.paper_title: MTFP MTFS - APPENDIX 3 CIPFA S114 appendix 3
findings.headline: Denbighshire overspent its budget in both 2022/23 and 2023/24, with corporate underspends masking service overspends
findings.detail: The council recorded overall budget overspends in two consecutive years. Service departments are systematically overspending and being offset by corporate department underspends. This cross-subsidy is a temporary solution that masks underlying service cost control problems.
findings.matters: Two consecutive years of overspend indicates systematic control failures or significant underestimation of service costs. When overspends are masked by corporate underspends, flexibility to absorb future pressures is depleted.
findings.figures: Overspends in 2022/23 and 2023/24; service overspends offset by corporate underspends in 2023/24 and 2024/25 (absolute figures not disclosed)
findings.quote: The Council found itself in an overall position of overspending against its budget in 2023/24 and 2022/23. It must be noted that it has been corporate underspends that have been funding service overspending in 2023/24 and 2024/25.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increasing by £9.3m in 2026/27, adding to long-term revenue obligations
findings.detail: The CFR is projected to increase by £9.3m during 2026/27 and remain elevated through 2028/29, reflecting capital spending financed through borrowing that will require repayment from revenue for decades. This growth commits future revenue to servicing debt rather than service delivery.
findings.matters: A growing CFR indicates the council is accumulating long-term debt obligations that constrain future financial flexibility. Each £1m of CFR requires approximately £50-60k annual revenue commitment for repayment and interest.
findings.figures: CFR increase of £9.3m in 2026/27; total CFR projected at £423.7m (2027) rising to £425.4m (2029)
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £9.3m during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council carries £327m debt at 4.7% average cost against investments earning only 3.89%
findings.detail: The council has £327m in borrowing at an average interest rate of 4.7% against only £31.5m in treasury investments earning 3.89%. This 81 basis point unfavorable spread is paid out of the revenue budget annually and represents a structural drag on finances as long as debt exceeds investments.
findings.matters: For a lender, this shows the council carries substantial debt and has minimal liquid reserves to offset it. The unfavorable rate spread indicates the council's historical borrowing has been expensive; if future rates rise, this spread widens further.
findings.figures: £327m borrowing @ 4.7% average; £31.5m treasury investments @ 3.89%; 81 basis point spread
findings.quote: Due to decisions taken in the past, at the time of writing the Council has £327m borrowing at an average interest rate of 4.7% and £31.5m treasury investments at an average rate of 3.89%.

findings.headline: Gross debt is growing faster than the Capital Financing Requirement, halving the council's compliance margin by 2029
findings.detail: Projected debt grows from £360.2m in 2026/27 to £393.4m in 2028/29 while the CFR grows from £423.7m to only £425.4m. The gap between debt and CFR shrinks from £63.5m to £32m—a 50% reduction. Statutory guidance requires debt to remain below CFR; the narrowing margin leaves little room for unexpected borrowing needs.
findings.matters: A narrowing debt-to-CFR ratio indicates the council is approaching its structural debt ceiling. This limits its ability to respond to capital emergencies and suggests future capital spending may be constrained, constraining the council's strategic flexibility.
findings.figures: Debt/CFR gap shrinks from £63.5m (2027) to £32m (2029); debt growing £33m while CFR grows only £1.7m
findings.quote: Statutory guidance is that debt should remain below the capital financing requirement, except in the short-term. As can be seen from Table 4, the Council expects to comply with this in the medium-term.

findings.headline: Capital receipts declined 87% from £3.75m in 2024/25 to £515k planned for 2026/27, requiring capital spend to be financed from grants, contributions or borrowing
findings.detail: The council received £3.75m from asset disposals in 2024/25 but has planned only £515k in capital receipts for 2026/27—an 87% decline. With capital receipts now minimal, capital expenditure must be financed entirely from grants, contributions, or new borrowing rather than property sales.
findings.matters: Capital receipts don't require revenue repayment. Their collapse forces the council to borrow more and commit revenue budget to servicing debt for decades, reducing financial flexibility and permanently increasing the cost of capital.
findings.figures: £3.75m capital receipts in 2024/25; £515k planned for council fund in 2026/27 (87% decline)
findings.quote: In 2024/25, £3.75m capital receipts were received from the sale of an agricultural estate, two pieces of land, some Council offices and a former lifeguard factory. A further £0.05m has been received so far in 2025/26. The Council has a programme of potential disposals which is reported to the Asset Management Group.

findings.headline: Nearly one-third of 2026/27 council fund capital is from unapproved estimated new projects
findings.detail: The capital plan includes £15.637m for estimated new projects that have not yet been approved by council. These include block allocations and Sustainable Communities for Learning schools projects. If approved, they will require financing, likely through additional borrowing; if not approved, the forecast is wrong.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the capital program. Material uncertainty about £15.6m of a £47.3m plan affects debt forecasting and reveals whether the council has clear visibility over committed capital.
findings.figures: £15.637m unapproved estimated new projects out of £47.285m total council fund capital (33%)
findings.quote: The estimated new projects include projects which are in the pipeline but have not been approved by Council , such as the block allocations and Sustainable Communities for Learning schools projects.

findings.headline: HRA applying maximum allowed rent increase due to rising costs but still facing a funding challenge
findings.detail: Welsh Government allows a maximum 4.3% rent increase (CPI 3.8% plus 0.5%). Denbighshire is recommending this maximum because of 'significantly rising standards and periods of significantly rising costs'. Critically, even with this maximum additional income, the council states it remains 'faced with a challenge to meet the required standards whilst also continuing to deliver much needed new homes.' The council must maintain and improve 3,334 homes to Welsh Housing Quality Standard and new Net Zero and Affordable Warmth targets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the HRA is operating at the maximum income constraint set by Welsh Government regulation, while still reporting a shortfall against investment needs for statutory housing standards and decarbonisation. This leaves no room for further income increases if costs continue rising.
findings.figures: 3,334 council homes; 4.3% maximum rent increase allowed (CPI 3.8% plus 0.5%)
findings.quote: Even with this additional income we are still faced with a challenge to meet the required standards whilst also continuing to deliver much needed new homes.

findings.headline: Building and construction cost inflation has significantly impacted housing capital programmes
findings.detail: The council reports significantly rising costs following the pandemic and high inflation period, with specific impact on building and construction sector costs affecting investment programmes. Both revenue and capital costs continue rising due to inflation, compounding pressure on budgets needed to meet new quality standards.
findings.matters: Sustained inflation in construction reduces the purchasing power of capital budgets and extends timelines to complete mandatory standard improvements, creating ongoing pressure on financial plans and potentially requiring future borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: No specific percentage increases for construction costs given; rent increase of 4.3% vs 2.7% previous year partially attributed to cost pressures
findings.quote: This has led to significant cost increases in the building & construction sector which has impacted on our investment programmes in our housing stock.

findings.headline: Mandated capital investment of £20m+ for housing standards can only be funded at maximum rent increase
findings.detail: The new Welsh Housing Quality Standard (WHQS 2023) requires significantly higher energy ratings for all homes. The council needs £20m to achieve WHQS 2 energy efficiency requirements, plus £8.91m backlog of works. The council explicitly states that any rent increase below the maximum allowed would reduce investment capability and extend timelines to meet standards, implying they are constrained by maximum rent levels.
findings.matters: Mandated capital standards create a funding gap that can only be closed through maximum rent increases, leaving no buffer for cost overruns. This suggests the council cannot afford required standards at lower rent levels, limiting financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £20m for WHQS 2 energy efficiency improvements; £8.91m backlog of works; 4.3% maximum rent increase
findings.quote: We need to spend an estimated £20m to achieve the additional WHQS 2 items to improve energy efficiency and affordable warmth for our households. In addition, due to disruption caused by the pandemic and subsequent inflationary cost increases, we have a backlog of works costing £8.91m.

findings.headline: Council expresses explicit concerns about the sustainability of HRA borrowing levels
findings.detail: The council states it has had to borrow significantly to fund capital spend and now questions whether this borrowing is sustainable. They conducted a 'deep dive' review in 2025 to ensure the Housing Stock Business Plan remains financially viable. They note that 'further work is required on an ongoing basis to review our level of borrowing and the associated debt financing costs, and adjustments to capital budgets may be required to maintain the financial sustainability of the HRA.'
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the HRA can service debt obligations. The council's own stated concerns about sustainability indicate financial stress and suggest debt levels may be at the edge of what the HRA can support.
findings.figures: Borrowing levels and debt financing costs shown in graph; specific amounts not disclosed in text
findings.quote: We have concerns regarding how sustainable this level of borrowing it is for the HRA. Therefore, earlier in 2025, we carried out an initial 'deep dive' review of the Housing Stock Business Plan to ensure the HRA remains financially viable.

findings.headline: Service charge costs rising 10% to £3.15 per property per week, signalling inflation in communal service costs
findings.detail: Service charges for communal facilities (lighting, cleaning, door entry, fire safety, grounds maintenance) have increased to £567k total, with the average per-property charge rising from £2.86 to £3.15 per week. This 10% year-on-year increase reflects inflationary pressure on the costs of servicing communal housing facilities and will need to be recovered through tenant charges in a population 75% dependent on welfare support.
findings.matters: Rising service costs in a high welfare-dependency population create affordability and collection risk. The council is passing cost increases to tenants already receiving housing benefit, which limits headroom.
findings.figures: Total service chargeable costs: £567k. Average charge per property: £3.15 per week (up from £2.86).
findings.quote: Overall costs show an increase over last year to £567k. Individual properties may be subject to a varied charge. The average charge per property has increased to £3.15 per week (from £2.86 last year).

findings.headline: CFO signals ongoing review of HRA borrowing sustainability with potential capital budget adjustments needed
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer explicitly states that 'work continues on an ongoing basis to review the level of borrowing and the associated debt financing costs, and adjustments to capital budgets may be required to maintain the financial sustainability of the HRA.' This signals concern about whether current borrowing levels and capital investment plans can be sustained without further rebalancing. The HRA uses borrowing to fund new build and improvement programmes, but the CFO's statement suggests the trajectory may require capital budget constraints.
findings.matters: A lender to this council needs to know whether HRA borrowing is on a sustainable path. This statement indicates potential pressure on the capital programme and suggests the council may need to curtail investment to maintain debt serviceability.
findings.figures: Forecast HRA balance 2025/26: £813k. Minimum balance target: £750k.
findings.quote: However work continues on an ongoing basis to review the level of borrowing and the associated debt financing costs, and adjustments to capital budgets may be required to maintain the financial sustainability of the HRA.

news_drafts.headline: Denbighshire forecasts £5.2m overspend for 2026/27, with schools £5.4m over budget
news_drafts.lead:
Denbighshire County Council's Cabinet was told on 20 October that the council expects to end 2026/27 having spent £314.1m against a budget of £308.9m, a forecast overspend of £5.2m, or 1.7%. A forecast overspend is where a council expects to finish the year having spent more than it budgeted.

The schools budget, including the part of school funding the council does not pass directly to schools, is forecast at £103.9m against a budget of £98.5m. That is £5.4m, or 5.4%, over. It is the largest variance of any service in the budget summary, and it is larger than the overspend for the council as a whole.

The council's savings programme, the cuts and efficiencies it has committed to in order to balance its budget, set a target of £3.17m for 2026/27. The savings tracker shows £1.82m achieved, or 57.4%. A further £701k, 22.1%, is in progress. Proposals worth £648k, 20.4%, are marked "not achieved", and £738k of the target remains undelivered. The papers set out the figures but, in the extracts available, do not say how the council plans to close the gap.
news_drafts.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary

news_drafts.headline: Denbighshire revised corporate income forecast down by £28.2m to £1.1m and matched cuts to expenditure, keeping overall budget overspend at £510k
news_drafts.lead: Denbighshire Council has revised its corporate income forecast from £29.3m to £1.1m mid-year and made equivalent cuts to expenditure, leaving its net budget position unchanged. The £28.2m reduction in expected income — roughly nine-tenths of what was budgeted — has been matched by spending reductions of the same scale, keeping the council's overall budget overspend at £510k (0.2%) against a total budget of £309m. The adjustment reflects changed circumstances for income sources, though the council has not detailed which. Service-level overspends are modest: Adult Social Care and Homelessness, the largest service budget at £67.8m, is forecast to overspend by £442k; Planning, Public Protection and Countryside by £268k on a £12.2m budget. The overall position has deteriorated by £402k from the previous forecast.
news_drafts.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary
